Title: Agentic Engineering Platforms
Abstract: What does a platform need when AI agents start writing code, running tests, and shipping changes? This talk looks at how engineering platforms can give agents the context, tools, and guardrails they need to work effectively. Jimmy will discuss how developer workflows, observability, and platform design can help teams adopt agents while keeping engineers in control.

Title: Before You Pick an Agent Orchestrator: What I Learned Wiring a Self-Driving SDLC
Abstract: Everyone's wiring AI agents into pipelines. Almost nobody tells you the orchestration layer is where it makes or breaks. I built a self-driving SDLC that specs, codes, tests, reviews and ships. To get there I battle-tested durable execution: Temporal, Restate, Inngest, LangGraph, DAG schedulers and more. I came back with scars to save you the trip. No orchestrator is a free lunch - each is great at one thing and painful at another - and I'll map the tradeoffs. Then the part that bites whichever you pick: durable execution wants a world that never changes; an LLM invents a new answer every time. Keep them apart - a thin controller that picks the next step, the real work (model calls, file writes) outside it - or a crash re-runs your expensive model calls and pays twice. You'll walk away knowing which engine to grab and which to skip, the failures that find you no matter the tool, why your agents will lie about success - and an honest answer to whether it's all worth the price.

Title: From Prompt Engineering to Agent Engineering: When LLMs Can Take Action
Abstract: Prompt engineering started with a relatively simple challenge: how do we get language models to produce better, more consistent answers? But LLMs are no longer just answering prompts. We are connecting them to enterprise data, giving them identities and permissions, equipping them with tools, and enabling them to take actions. As we move from prompt-driven applications to agentic systems, the engineering problem changes with them. In this session, I’ll explore the shift from prompt engineering to agent engineering and what it means for anyone building LLM-powered applications. We’ll follow the journey from Prompt → Context → Identity → Tools → Action → Governance, looking at how each layer introduces new capabilities — and new failure modes. What happens when retrieved context contains malicious instructions? What changes when an agent can invoke an MCP tool or API? How should we think about the identity and permissions behind an agent? And how do we maintain visibility and control once agents move beyond generating text and start interacting with real systems? Drawing on practical experience from building enterprise AI agents and helping organizations secure and assess their agentic systems, I’ll share patterns for designing agents that are useful and capable without giving them unnecessary freedom. Attendees will leave with a practical mental model for evolving their approach from engineering better prompts to engineering the identities, context, tools, permissions, and controls surrounding the agents those prompts now power. Key Takeaways Attendees will learn: * Why prompt engineering alone is no longer enough for agentic AI * How prompts, context, identity, tools, and permissions combine in an agentic system * How tool calling and MCP change the security boundary of an LLM application * Why prompt injection and untrusted context become more consequential when agents can take actions * Practical principles for building controlled, observable, and secure AI agents * How to evolve from thinking only about prompt engineering to thinking about agent engineering

Title: Beyond the Claw: Building Your Personal Coding Agent
Abstract: Like a Roomba for your code, AI agents can coordinate to clean things up, fix bugs, and add new features. They can also keep working 24/7 while you're focused on something else. In this session, we'll look at what AI agents can actually do today and how a "Claw" turns them into a persistent workspace that can use tools, remember context, and run scheduled tasks. We'll go beyond coding to see how the same setup can help with research, planning, reminders, and other personal-assistant work. Along the way, we'll cover the current landscape, where these systems still fall short, and the approvals and guardrails that keep them useful. You'll leave with practical and fun ways to start using one without having to build everything from scratch.

Title: From Self-Service to Safe Autonomy: The Authority Shift
Abstract: Self-service was built around a simple assumption: someone already knows what they want the platform to do. AI breaks that assumption. An agent may detect degradation, decide a deployment caused it, and choose to roll it back—without anyone requesting the action. At that point, the platform is no longer just validating whether an action can be executed safely. It is being asked to trust the decision that the action should happen at all. That changes the platform contract. This session explores the shift from validating execution to validating intent. We’ll examine the boundary between an agent’s decision, the authority it receives, and the action the platform ultimately allows—using operational scenarios where autonomous systems can diagnose, remediate, or change production environments. The goal is not another layer of AI guardrails. It is to rethink what self-service becomes when the consumer of the platform can create its own intent. Self-service asks: “Can I do this?” Safe autonomy adds the harder question: “Should I be allowed to decide that this needs to be done?”

Title: The hidden infra behind "For You" pages: Real-time AI personalization
Abstract: AI personalization for apps with a large and global user base is a difficult engineering challenge. Global companies like Tripadvisor, Medium, and ShareChat depend on highly available, low-latency AI infrastructure to deliver hotel recommendations, "For You" feed items and relevant short-form video content. In this talk, we cover the underlying systems that power these user facing recommendation use cases. - Running real-time model inference with millisecond latency - Setting up a centralized feature store that feeds both training and serving - Leveraging OSS feature store frameworks and tools - Best-practice data modeling approaches for online inference to minimize latency - Cost-effective utilization of cold/object storage, hot caches, and low-latency databases for model training and user-facing inference - Meeting strict SLAs (p90, p95, p99, etc) By the end, attendees will learn how to design AI infrastructure that serves fresh features in milliseconds. They will also see real data models, latency numbers, and cost trade-offs from three production systems.

Title: How Many Judgments Can One LLM Make Before It Fails?
Abstract: Platform teams building shared LLM evaluation services face a practical cost question: should each criterion get its own judge call, or should one call return several scores? Packing criteria reduces repeated input, but a cheaper evaluation service is only useful if its measurements remain informative. I built an experiment that keeps the criteria constant while varying how many share a call. The design randomizes criterion grouping and order, preserves the output budget per criterion, and tracks agreement with human labels alongside tied scores. In the documented five-criterion pilot, cost per thousand criteria fell from $0.593 to $0.318, with no statistically detectable accuracy change. That finding is specific to the comparison; it is not proof of equivalence or a universal packing limit. This talk walks through the experimental controls, a rubric-anchoring failure, and the limits of extending the study with synthetic corruptions. Attendees will leave with a method for testing a packing change before adopting it in a shared evaluation pipeline, including what to hold constant, which quality and cost measures to report, and when the evidence is too weak to justify rollout.

Title: Building the Internal Developer Platform (IDP) for Generative AI: From Foundation Models to Self-Service APIs
Abstract: As engineering organizations scale generative AI across product teams, platform architects face rapid enterprise sprawl: fragmented and leaked provider API keys, duplicate vector stores, zero granular cost attribution, and uncoordinated rate-limiting throttles. Treating third-party LLMs and private model clusters as ad-hoc microservice dependencies turns AI infrastructure into an unmanageable financial and operational risk. This session delivers an end-to-end architectural blueprint for treating Generative AI as a managed, self-service Internal Developer Platform (IDP) primitive. We dissect the construction of an enterprise GenAI reverse proxy and gateway layer that decouples client applications from underlying foundation models. We examine the mechanics of high-throughput semantic caching using Redis Vector Search and HNSW indexing, demonstrating how cosine similarity lookups eliminate redundant inferences to slash p95 latencies by 40–60% and mitigate upstream provider quota limits. Next, we implement declarative Policy-as-Code guardrails (Open Policy Agent / Envoy) directly in the ingress path to enforce tenant-level token budgets, model whitelisting, and automated PII/sensitive data redaction. Finally, we integrate OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions to propagate trace context, giving platform teams line-rate FinOps visibility into prompt/completion token consumption attributed directly to Kubernetes namespaces and cost centers. Key Attendee Takeaways: - Centralized GenAI Gateway Pattern: Architectural patterns to abstract hosted and private foundation models behind a resilient, unified multi-tenant proxy handling failover, dynamic load balancing, and secret vaulting. - Semantic Caching at Scale: How vector-similarity caching with Redis intercepts repetitive queries, drastically curbing external token consumption and cutting API latency by 40–60%. - Policy-as-Code & Observability Pipeline: Implementing OPA filters for budget quotas and data masking alongside OpenTelemetry distributed tracing to map token spend directly to tenant namespaces.

Title: Building an In-House Real-Time Telemetry Platform: From Raw Game State Integration to 31% Conversion Gains
Abstract: Relying on third-party data vendors for critical real-time features often leads to latency spikes, missing events, and lost revenue. When external feeds delayed esports draft updates by minutes, we built our own internal telemetry streaming platform from the ground up. In this talk, I will share how BetBoom designed an in-house real-time platform using Dota 2 Game State Integration (GSI), Go, WebSockets, and gRPC to process low-level game snapshots and stream live pick/ban events directly to millions of users. I will talk about: 1. How to turn unordered, repeating HTTP snapshots into a deterministic sequence of stateful business events. 2. Implementing JWT-authenticated telemetry intake, PostgreSQL transactional state management, and real-time WebSocket broadcasting. 3. Designing an internal platform compatible with legacy third-party contracts, enabling seamless automated fallback. 4. Business Impact: How moving to an in-house telemetry platform scaled to 5M+ views and quadrupled user conversion from 8.4% to 31.2%.

Title: Beyond the First Pipeline: Scaling Data Pipelines Across Teams
Abstract: Many organisations start their CDC journey with just a few pipelines. Then more teams adopt it, new use cases emerge, and the platform team ends up spending its time reviewing configurations, deploying connectors, troubleshooting issues, and handling tickets. The problem is no longer CDC itself, but how it can scale. Debezium Platform addresses this challenge by providing an abstraction around sources, destinations, transformations, and pipelines. Platform teams can offer a self-service experience that allows data engineers to create and manage pipelines, while Debezium Platform takes care of deployment, operations, monitoring, and observability. In this talk, we'll explore how Debezium Platform helps standardise CDC adoption across teams and provides a consistent way to deploy, operate, and observe pipelines at scale. In the live demo, we'll see how data from a single database can be consumed by three teams with different needs. We'll create and deploy pipelines for each use case and see how the platform manages their lifecycle, health, and observability from a single place.

Title: Platform Engineering for Real-Time Bidding Under Strict Latency Constraints
Abstract: Real-Time Bidding systems put platform engineering under extreme pressure. Each advertising opportunity must pass through targeting, decisioning, bidding, and response generation within a strict latency budget, while the underlying platform handles large volumes of concurrent traffic reliably. This session explores the platform engineering patterns behind production-grade RTB systems, focusing on how low-latency services can remain scalable, resilient, observable, and safe to evolve. We’ll examine a modular auction architecture spanning feature retrieval, targeting, decisioning, bid strategy, and response generation. The session explores latency budgets as architectural constraints, along with timeout and fallback mechanisms that prevent downstream dependencies from delaying critical request paths. It also covers practical approaches for evolving live infrastructure using traffic mirroring, controlled traffic splitting, progressive deployments, CI/CD automation, and production observability. Attendees will leave with practical architectural patterns for operating and modernizing latency-sensitive platforms while maintaining reliability and minimizing disruption to live traffic.

Title: Platform Engineering for Resilient Retail Supply Chains with Event-Driven Design
Abstract: Modern retail platforms must continuously respond to changing demand, real-time inventory updates, and distributed order fulfillment while remaining reliable, scalable, and easy to operate. This session explores how Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) provides a strong foundation for platform engineering by enabling resilient, loosely coupled systems that support business-critical retail operations. Using a retail supply chain as the reference architecture, the session examines practical design decisions behind event sourcing, publish-subscribe communication, and Apache Kafka for connecting services responsible for inventory, logistics, and order management. It also discusses how architectural patterns such as Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) and the Saga pattern help coordinate distributed workflows while maintaining consistency across microservices. Beyond the architecture itself, the presentation focuses on the platform engineering considerations that influence day-to-day operations, including scalability, fault tolerance, asynchronous processing, event ordering, eventual consistency, and service evolution. The session also shares practical lessons from designing event-driven platforms, highlighting common implementation challenges, architectural tradeoffs, and approaches that improve maintainability and operational resilience. Attendees will leave with actionable insights into designing event-driven platforms that simplify service integration, improve system reliability, and support high-volume retail supply chain workloads while maintaining scalability, resilience, and long-term maintainability. This version is a stronger fit for Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026 because it: Aligns with the CFP's emphasis on real-world architecture decisions and lessons learned. Highlights platform engineering concerns such as scalability, reliability, maintainability, and service evolution. Focuses on practical implementation rather than theory. Preserves your original retail supply chain and Event-Driven Architecture context without introducing unsupported or fabricated content.

Title: Building an Internal Mobile Platform: A Plugin-Based Dev Mode Framework
Abstract: As mobile products scale, internal developer tools multiply rapidly—feature toggles, environment switchers, mock push generators, diagnostic screens, and dynamic API endpoints. Initially built ad-hoc, these utilities become scattered across debug menus and hidden gestures, causing friction for developers, QA engineers, and analysts across projects. In this talk, Denis Galkin presents the architecture of a unified, plugin-based Dev Mode framework designed as an internal platform product. Drawing from real-world fintech application infrastructure, Denis breaks down the separation of concerns between framework and product code: the core framework handles activation UI, routing (via Navigation 3), and plugin registration contracts, while individual feature teams retain full autonomy over plugin business logic. Listeners will learn how standardizing internal tooling as a reusable SDK improves cross-application consistency, accelerates QA workflows, and reduces developer friction.

Title: A Platform Team of One, With AI
Abstract: AI can help you build a side project quickly. The harder question is whether you can operate it without becoming its permanent support team. Drawing from my experiments building and running multiple projects alongside a full-time job, I’ll describe the problem as a platform-engineering problem at a team size of one: reducing repeated work, making delegation usable, and deciding which tasks deserve human attention. I’ll share what worked and what failed when I used AI beyond coding, automated routine work, and built tools and controls around the projects. The talk focuses on the operating model after launch, with practical takeaways for developers who want more independent projects without more obligations.

Title: Beyond AI Coding: The New Bottlenecks of Software Delivery
Abstract: AI coding tools radically change one part of software delivery: producing code. But when code reaches pull requests and pipelines faster, teams often discover that their real constraints are elsewhere: environments, tests, security controls, reviews, approvals, service ownership, deployment practices, and production feedback. The result is a familiar failure mode: more activity, more work in progress, and not necessarily more value shipped. This talk shows how platform teams can make those constraints visible before AI turns speed into larger queues. We will map the delivery path, identify signals that work is waiting rather than moving, and use platform capabilities—golden paths, paved CI/CD, policy as code, self-service environments, and delivery telemetry—to remove friction at the current constraint. AI is not the enemy; it is a stress test for the delivery system.

Title: Mobile as a Platform: How Five Autonomous Teams Ship into One 53-Million-User App
Abstract: Platform engineering is usually discussed in terms of cloud infrastructure, but a large mobile app faces the same problem inside a single binary. On T-Mobile's T-Life app, which serves 53 million active users, five engineering PODs with more than 50 mobile engineers build account, payments, IoT, and loyalty features. Without a platform layer, cross-module dependencies caused cascading build failures and release bottlenecks. This talk shows how the core app shell was treated as an internal platform with clear contracts for the teams building on it: Versioned interface contracts that let modules evolve independently Independent build pipelines that isolate one team's failures from the others A modular feature-injection framework as a self-service path for shipping features Governance that balances team autonomy with platform stability Reactive MVI/MVVM state patterns that keep data consistent without tight coupling The approach delivered zero build regression across teams and helps sustain a crash-free session rate above 99.9%. Attendees leave with patterns for building an internal mobile platform that scales with the organization.

Title: Make your app its own sandbox
Abstract: Can an application become its own sandbox? A document parser should not automatically inherit the same operating-system permissions as an HTTP client. Yet components within a JVM application commonly share the privileges of the entire process. This talk introduces MazeWall, an experimental open-source toolkit that lets Java and Kotlin applications define their own restrictions, enforced by the Linux kernel. Combining seccomp, Landlock, and the JDK Foreign Function & Memory API, MazeWall applies different syscall and filesystem policies to selected workloads. Practical examples will show how runtime profiling helps generate policy candidates, how kernel-enforced restrictions can limit the impact of malicious inputs, and when separate worker processes are needed for stronger isolation. The presentation examines how application-aware sandboxing complements containers, its performance and deployment trade-offs, and its security limitations. Attendees will learn how to give application components fewer privileges—and why restricting a thread is not the same as isolating arbitrary hostile code.

Title: The Paved Road Had a Compliance Gate
Abstract: Platform teams measure success in adoption. Mine is used by more than 150 product teams across 200 markets. Adoption was the easy part. The hard design problem was deciding what the platform would refuse to do. I own a Model Context Protocol server at PayPal that exposes three tools in front of the internationalization layer. Product teams use it to get correct address formats, name order, official government identifiers and ISO 20022 message structure for a market without first becoming experts in that market. An integration that used to take a two-week sprint now takes three hours. This talk covers the part of platform engineering that does not fit the golden-path story: what happens when your consumers are AI agents instead of engineers, and the paved road has to carry a compliance gate. Permission scoping per market. The failure modes we hit when a tool call was confidently correct about the wrong market. And how you show an auditor what a self-service platform did two years ago.

Title: Building Guardrails for AI-Generated Frontends: A Platform Engineering Approach
Abstract: AI coding assistants can generate frontend code quickly, but speed does not guarantee that the resulting interface follows the engineering standards a team depends on. Accessibility, testing, component consistency, and maintainability can easily become issues that engineers discover only after the code has already been generated. This talk explores how platform engineering principles can be applied to AI-assisted frontend development. Using accessibility as a practical example, I’ll show how reusable components, design-system constraints, automated testing, Storybook, Playwright, axe-core, and CI checks can create a paved path that guides both developers and AI coding tools toward better implementations. We’ll compare three approaches: relying on AI-generated code as-is, adding standards through prompting, and enforcing engineering expectations through architecture-level guardrails. I’ll also cover where these guardrails help, where they fall short, and what teams should consider as AI-generated code becomes a larger part of everyday development. Attendees will leave with practical ideas for evolving developer platforms so that AI-generated code follows more of the same standards expected from human-written code.

Title: Kubernetes, LLM and Platform Engineer walk into a bar
Abstract: A platform engineer, an LLM, and Kubernetes walk into a bar. The platform engineer wants reproducibility. The LLM wants 80GB of VRAM and a GPU that isn't already taken. Kubernetes wants everything to be a declarative object with a reconciler. Nobody gets what they want — at least not on the first try. This talk is about what it actually takes to build Model-as-a-Service on top of OpenEverest: serving models with KServe and vLLM, routing through a unified AI gateway with per-model keys and token quotas, splitting models across multiple nodes when they don't fit on one GPU, and autoscaling inference based on real traffic. We'll show the architecture, the failure modes we hit, and the parts that turned out to be harder than expected. If you're a platform engineer who's been handed "we need to run LLMs on our cluster" and told to figure it out, this is the talk we wish we'd had.

Title: Monitoring is still the one thing nobody automated
Abstract: Your platform team automated the repo scaffold, the pipeline, the secrets, the infrastructure, the dashboards. Then someone ships a service and monitoring gets set up by a human, later, by hand, in a web UI, if anyone remembers. That gap is why so many services run for months with either no monitoring or the wrong monitoring. It isn't a tooling problem so much as a workflow one. Monitoring sits outside the golden path, so it depends on discipline instead of defaults. I work on monitoring, and this talk is about closing that gap from the command line. I'll walk through creating and managing monitors as part of a deploy rather than after it, what belongs in a template versus what genuinely varies per service, and the small operational details that bite you the first time, like which credentials have write permissions and which required flags people always forget. I'll also be honest about where a CLI is the wrong answer, and what monitoring you genuinely can't template because it depends on things your service doesn't own. Useful if you own a platform and want new services to arrive already being watched.

Title: Platform SLOs Beyond Uptime: Measuring the Journey from Request to Value
Abstract: Platform teams frequently measure availability, latency and infrastructure utilization while overlooking whether developers can successfully use the platform. A platform can meet every operational SLO and still impose days of waiting, repeated support requests and unnecessary cognitive load. This presentation introduces journey-based platform SLOs that measure the complete path from a developer’s request to a usable, policy-compliant capability. Examples include time to first environment, self-service completion rate, failed-workflow recovery time, support dependency, rework rate and time to operational readiness. Using a multi-cloud tenant-provisioning journey as a practical example, the session shows how platform teams can combine technical telemetry with developer-experience outcomes. Attendees will leave with a framework for selecting platform indicators that demonstrate whether a golden path is genuinely faster, safer and easier—not merely available.

Title: Designing a Self-Healing Ops Platform: Telemetry, RAG, and Confidence-Gated AI Agents
Abstract: Enterprise IT platforms often combine monitoring, endpoint management, and ITSM tools that never talk to each other. The result is a support model that stays reactive, even though up to 40% of Level-1 demand stems from issues existing telemetry could anticipate. This talk breaks down the Autonomous Digital Operations Framework (ADOF), a conceptual six-layer reference architecture, layer by layer. It covers: How endpoint telemetry and ITSM data are unified into one signal layer How Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) gives agents access to enterprise knowledge How six specialized agents divide responsibility, including Incident Prediction, Asset Health, and Procurement Intelligence The core design decision is a confidence gate. Composite scores for enterprise health, business impact, and automation confidence decide whether an agent executes a fix (above 85%) or routes it for human approval (below 60%). A five-level maturity model sets how autonomy expands over time. ADOF is proposed for future validation, with illustrative targets such as up to a 40% reduction in repetitive Level-1 requests. Viewers will leave with a reference architecture and practical design patterns for building proactive, governed automation into their own platforms.

Title: Platform Migrations Without the Downtime: An Engineering Playbook
Abstract: Platform engineering teams are increasingly the ones owning the hardest kind of project: replacing a legacy system the business depends on every hour of every day. This talk presents a practitioner-built architecture playbook for exactly that problem, drawn from real migrations of enterprise order management, healthcare claims, and CRM platforms. It covers three core patterns platform teams can build as reusable internal capability — dual-write parallel-run architecture, bidirectional synchronization for legacy/new system consistency, and change data capture for scalable incremental data movement — along with a five-dimension maturity framework (latency, reliability, bidirectionality, scalability, migration safety) for assessing whether an internal platform is actually ready to support a major cutover. Forrester-cited data shows event-driven approaches can cut data latency from hours to milliseconds; attendees will leave with criteria for building this as platform capability rather than reinventing it project by project.

Title: AI Maintenance Platforms for Reliable Power Plant Operations
Abstract: Power plants depend on the continuous performance of critical assets such as turbines, generators, boilers, and transformers, where a single forced outage can affect operational cost, grid reliability, and safety. However, traditional reactive and time-based maintenance approaches often fall short because they do not fully account for real operating conditions, asset degradation patterns, and complex system interactions. This session presents AI-driven maintenance as a practical platform engineering challenge for modern power plant operations. Instead of treating predictive maintenance as isolated models or standalone analytics, the talk explains how AI capabilities can be built into scalable reliability platforms that connect plant data, diagnostics, workflows, observability, and decision support. The session examines how machine learning, deep learning, expert systems, and natural language processing can be applied across major plant systems. Examples include vibration and bearing diagnostics for rotating machinery, combustion and heat transfer modeling for boilers and HRSGs, dissolved gas analysis for transformers, and AI-assisted alarm filtering to reduce operator overload. The discussion also covers the platform design choices required to make these capabilities usable in real operations, including data pipeline reliability, legacy system integration, explainability, cybersecurity controls, governance, and maintainable workflows. Attendees will gain practical insight into what it takes to move from reactive maintenance and disconnected analytics toward a more integrated AI-enabled asset reliability platform. The talk shares a structured five-step implementation framework, highlights adoption barriers such as data quality gaps and integration complexity, and concludes with future-facing capabilities such as digital twins, autonomous inspection robotics, and enterprise-wide asset analytics. The goal is to provide engineers, architects, and platform practitioners with clear, practical takeaways for building and operating AI-driven maintenance systems that improve reliability, reduce maintenance friction, and support safer, more sustainable power generation.

Title: Terraform and Ansible Are Not an Architecture
Abstract: Many platform teams can say they use Terraform, Ansible, CI/CD and source-of-truth systems. Fewer can clearly explain how infrastructure change is approved, executed, validated, recovered and handed over when something goes wrong. This talk argues that tools are not the architecture. The architecture is the operating model around them: how intent is captured, how execution is controlled, how governance decisions are made, and how recovery evidence is preserved. Using HybridOps as a practical public example, Jeleel Muibi will show how infrastructure automation can move beyond scripts and pipelines into a governed operating surface for hybrid environments. The focus is not on promoting a tool, but on the pattern behind reliable platform engineering: separating intent, execution, governance and implementation so infrastructure becomes easier to operate, audit and recover. Attendees will learn: why automation tools alone do not create a platform operating model; how source-of-truth data, validation gates and execution boundaries reduce operational risk; how recovery evidence and structured documentation make infrastructure easier to hand over, review and improve.
